TLDR;

The Danger List

Your robots.txt "Do Not Scrape" signs become legally useless: robots.txt is just a voluntary preference, not a law. While Meta says in PR statements that it will respect robots.txt, it left that promise out of the binding legal contract. By keeping your business account active, you are signing a contract that legally authorizes Meta to ignore your site’s block-lists.

- Meta can create fake accounts to bypass registration walls: The terms explicitly authorize Meta to "create test credentials" to crawl your site. Legal experts warn this gives Meta permission to sign up as a fake user to scrape gated content behind login screens or basic paywalls that anonymous bots usually can't see.

- Your entire domain is fair game, not just links you post: Because the terms cover any domain "associated with your products or services" (or shared by regular users on Meta), Meta isn't just scraping the specific landing pages you run ads for—it has a green light to crawl your entire website from top to bottom.

- AI training is still allowed through a backdoor: Removing the word "train" is a PR smokescreen. The contract still lets Meta scrape your site to "develop, improve, and research... advertising and business products." Because "business products" isn't strictly defined—and Meta builds AI tools for businesses "developing" legally covers training AI models on your proprietary articles, data, and work.

- Third-party companies get the same access: The terms grant these scraping rights to "any entity acting on our behalf," meaning external contractors or third-party scraping vendors hired by Meta also have legal cover to harvest your site.

- It is a non-negotiable hostage situation (Zero Opt-Out): There is no toggle or form to reject this before the October 30 deadline. Your only legal way to decline is to completely delete your commercial presence across Facebook, Instagram, Threads, and WhatsApp—forcing you to choose between surrendering your content for free or losing access to your audience.

The Bottom Line: Starting October 30, their updated terms give it sweeping permission to scrape entire websites linked to any Meta Business account (Facebook, Instagram, Threads, WhatsApp). Despite a last-minute wording tweak after backlash, legal experts warn the rules still let Meta harvest publisher content to build AI tools—with zero option to opt out.

1. What Exact Things Can Meta Do?

If you have a Meta Business account, you authorize Meta (and its third-party partners) to:

a) Deploy automated bots: Use web scrapers, crawlers, spiders, and user agents on your site. b) Bypass basic walls: Create "test credentials" to access, index, cache, analyze, and collect your content. c) Monitor continuously: Periodically pull updates from your domains, web pages, and URLs.

2. What is the Extent of the Scraping? - What gets scraped: Any domain, webpage, URL, or content "associated with" your business or shared by users on Meta platforms. Legal experts note this is broad enough to let Meta scrape entire websites, not just specific landing pages. - - Who it affects: Virtually every news organization and business that uses a Meta account to manage Facebook Pages, Instagram profiles, Threads, or WhatsApp channels.

How it expanded:

  - Previously: Meta could only scrape your site if you specifically used its generative AI ad features, and only to "optimize your ads."
 
  - Now: It applies to all business accounts by default, and scraped data can be used for all "advertising and business products" (plus platform security/integrity).
3. Why Legal Experts Say Meta's "Fix" Changes Nothing After initial outrage, Meta revised the text on Friday to remove the word "train" and claimed it still respects robots.txt (the code websites use to block scrapers). Legal experts aren't buying it for three reasons:

- "Develop" still means "Train": Meta replaced "train" with permission to "develop, improve, research, and maintain advertising and business products." Attorneys point out that "business products" isn't strictly defined, and "developing" AI business tools naturally includes training AI models on your data.

- The robots.txt loophole: While a Meta spokesperson publicly promised to respect robots.txt flags, Meta refused to put that promise into the actual legal terms. Because robots.txt is voluntary, signing a contract that explicitly authorizes scraping legally overrides your robots.txt preferences.

- Take it or leave it: There is no opt-out. To avoid giving Meta permission to scrape their websites, businesses and news outlets would have to abandon Facebook, Instagram, Threads, and WhatsApp entirely before October 30.

I believe it has to do with the age of the 911 system. Older systems do not support remote location, microphone and camera access.

Apparently the US 911 system integrated some Israeli tech from a company founded by Israeli intelligence personnel called Reporty Homeland Security that later rebranded as Carbyne. Carbyne was headed by former Israeli prime minister Ehud Barak. The company, received much of its initial funding from Jeffery Epstein and Ehud Barak.

I don't know if any of the Israeli tech is running on handsets, but it is definitely running on the back-end in the US 911 emergency call systems. The on-device portion of the 911 emergency calling that grants remote access to location, video, and microphone is part of the closed, proprietary, Google Play Services, on Android.

If running a de-googled rom, you will presumably not be sending any location data or providing other access to your phone when calling 911.

Someone who is usually reliable stated that Scott Bessent had strong ties to this company, Ahud Barrak, and Jeffery Epstien (and was instrumental in getting Carbyne's tech adopted by US 911 system). But, I have not found evidence documenting Bessent's ties to Carbyne. If someone knows more about this-- either confirming or definitively refuting, please share.

comment_text.value:
There is not some arbitrary notion of wheel reinvention just for browsers. Calling browsers 'just browsers' is doing their feature set a huge disservice: they are bona fide operating systems or virtual machines, which have to load and run untrusted, unverified data and code within critical system libraries (many of which with kernel-mode access, such as GPU drivers, sound drivers, USB subsystems, and more), and do a huge amount of sandboxing to guard against escalations.

Within Google, a Chromium build uses remote build execution by default, upstream Clang by default (for the latest features and fixes, and Chromium developers regularly contribute to LLVM), and needs to cross-compile easily for at least a dozen different OS-architecture triples (Linux x86-64, Linux ARM, macOS, Windows x86-64, Windows on ARM, iOS, Android x86-64, Android ARM, Android TV, some BSDs, etc).

Everything you've listed—from ninja, to Clang, to libraries with custom patches, to Clang releases, including requiring pre-releases sometimes—is optimised for Google's scale, rather than the lone warrior developer. What you call 'sane Linux defaults' (especially the examples you have listed: GCC, automake, so-called 'system libraries') are highly antagonistic to all of the above.

They may make life easy for the so-called 'default case' of desktop Linux (arguable; Chromium was first released on Windows, and secondly since desktop Linux's most common C library, glibc has an unstable ABI, making back-portability impossible), but make it incredibly hard to get out a project of such immense complexity. All of Chromium's tooling and 'complexity' was developed in response to the 'sane' defaults being not so sane after all.

To get a GCC cross-compile for a given set of architecture triples, one needs a complete graph of GCC toolchains targeting every pair of host and target. On the other hand Clang is natively a cross-compiler; pass in `--sysroot` and the host compiler will redirect for the target instantly. Automake (and the autotools in general) is slow as molasses compared to ninja. It is based on computing and compilation from the 1970s, and their defaults probe for long-since-dead string comparison functions that are expected to work by default nowadays on most hosted systems. Not to mention it has an extraordinarily complicated configure step[1], and an equally appalling macro-based configure language.

Ninja is purely declarative, and is not even meant to be human-readable, as it is a back-end for a variety of build generator tools (CMake, XMake, build2, Bazel (Blaze internally at Google), Meson, probably more). Google have in fact rewritten Ninja to be a remote-build-capable tool from the outset[2], and they call it Siso. Siso has more than halved my Android build times even compared to Ninja because of its incredible use of RBE.

Frankly I think it should be evident why they have opted for 'rewriting the world' including vendoring and modifying system libraries, as well as including efforts like Skia, ANGLE, and more: directly relying on 'system libraries' is painful. I mentioned GPU drivers. Imagine rewriting the same code over and over to have precisely the same behaviour on D3D, Vulkan, OpenGL, Metal, and every single vendor GPU driver on every single system (and there are a lot more on mobile than on desktop: ARM Mali, Qualcomm Adreno, Samsung Xclipse, Imagination PowerVR, Huawei, MediaTek; this is not even close to exhaustive, just look at the Khronos vendor list).

When comments like yours are made I wonder if there is ever a consideration beyond 'it makes the developer's life hard'. As developers, our ultimate target audience are the users of our software. We should be willing to do anything come hell or high water, even making the dev-ex extraordinarily convoluted, if it means the user experience will be the smoothest and fastest possible. Sure, there is a balance, but I believe it should be strongly skewed towards the user story first.

[1]: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/84/Autoconf...

[2]: https://chromium.googlesource.com/build/+/refs/heads/main/si...

Most "AI engineering" is still engineering. Retries, idempotency, a human gate where the model isn't sure. The model is the easy part.

I had the idea for BIGWORDS.PAGE when I wanted to display a message on a tablet that I had remote management control over, but no physical access. Configuring it to be a kiosk browser is easy, but how do I get the browser to show my message? So I made the URL be the message.

It uses a URL fragment to configure the message. Browsers don't send URL fragments to the server, so I never see your message. There's no backend, and no storage.

All parameters are documented, so generating a message link is easy. There's also a built-in editor to make it extra easy.

https://bigwords.page/#Hello,%20HN!&bg=ff6600&fg=000000&font...

There are a few extra features like slides, animations, and countdowns and timers. QR codes too. Not too fancy, but hopefully enough to be useful.

I know the uses for this are pretty niche. But it may be one of those things that you keep as a nugget in your brain, a tool in your back pocket. Not something you use often, but when you do it makes things just a little bit easier.

It's open source (MIT), and self-hostable if that's your thing.

Let me know what you think.
